match.reason: The bank point teaches how context shapes an argument's tone, language and evidence, but it does not cover how voice, sound, images and editing position an audience in audio and video, so the new point needs its own card.

draft.title: Argument in audio and video
card: Audio and video texts persuade with more than words. Voice, sound, images and editing all work with the script to position the audience.
the speaker's pace, pitch, volume and pauses. A slow, low voice can sound serious. A fast, rising voice can sound urgent or excited.
music, sound effects, colour, framing and what is shown on screen. Soft piano over an empty classroom can create sadness or concern.
the order and length of shots and sounds. Quick cuts can build pressure. A long shot held on one face can invite sympathy.
draft.remember: Analyse how voice, sound, images and editing work with the words to shape the audience's response.

a.q: In a podcast, a presenter slows down and lowers her voice as she says the town's last library may close. What is the likely effect?
opts: It signals seriousness and invites concern
It signals excitement and invites celebration
It shows the presenter is unsure of her facts
It makes the audience focus on the music instead
a.why: A slow, low voice usually sounds serious, so listeners are positioned to treat the closure as a real loss. Excitement is tempting, but that is more often shown by a fast, rising voice.
a.clue: Think about what a slow, low voice sounds like.

b.q: A video against litter shows a calm beach, then cuts rapidly between plastic bags, a gull's nest and a turtle, with a harsh drumbeat getting faster. How does the editing help the argument?
opts: Fast cuts build urgency and pressure to act
Fast cuts make the beach seem calm and safe
Fast cuts show the filmmaker has no clear view
Fast cuts give the audience time to reflect slowly
b.why: Rapid cuts, with the quickening drumbeat, create a sense of pressure and alarm, which can push viewers toward acting on the problem. A calm effect is wrong because the pace is fast, and reflection comes more from long, held shots.
b.clue: What does a rising pace of cuts do to the mood?

a.best: It signals seriousness and invites concern

b.best: Fast cuts build urgency and pressure to act
